extracted.intended_audience: researchers, graduate students, and scholars in foundations of mathematics, logic, and philosophy of mathematics (constructivism vs classical mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of foundational and methodological standards distinguishing Bishopian constructivism, other varieties of constructivism, and classical/post-LEM mathematical practice, with emphasis on concepts such as numerical meaning, LEM, choice, continuity, and pedagogical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical meaning (constructive sine qua non)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical statements and methods must have 'numerical meaning' — that is, constructive content/witnessing information rather than reliance on non-constructive principles such as LEM or LPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop treats lack of numerical meaning as the central defect of classical/non-constructive mathematics; numerical meaning corresponds to avoiding principles like LPO/LEM and providing explicit witnessing information. Examples and counterexamples are used throughout (e.g., reliance on axiom of choice hides such witnessing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Debasement of meaning (Bishop's critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of non-constructive methods (e.g., LEM, certain uses of choice, non-standard entities) constitutes a 'debasement' of mainstream mathematics' meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop's rhetoric brands non-constructive approaches (including non-standard analysis) as debasing meaning unless they can be shown to provide numerical/witnessing content; the authors analyze whether this charge is pedagogically or foundationally motivated and present examples where the critique is intelligible or problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity in Bishopian constructivism (verbal renaming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop accepts only uniformly continuous functions (on compact intervals) and renames them 'continuous' in his constructive framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This renaming yields 'verbal equality' with classical theorems while altering definitions; reviewers point out this may mislead readers. Subsequent constructive research shows other weaker continuity notions (e.g., sequential continuity) can arise naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: continuity vs uniform continuity (quantifier complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity (pointwise) and uniform continuity differ in definitional form: continuity can be defined via limits at a fixed point using 3 quantifiers, while uniform continuity requires 4 quantifiers handling pairs of points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogically, uniform continuity's additional quantifier increases conceptual difficulty; many textbooks present continuity after limits, while uniform continuity forces a return to epsilontics and is harder for undergraduates to grasp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical accessibility of epsilon-delta definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Epsilon-delta (ǫ, δ) definitions involve alternations of quantifiers and are intrinsically difficult for students; even explaining them for linear functions may consume a semester in some case studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactive approaches can help but the intrinsic difficulty of alternations of quantifiers makes full mastery challenging; this pedagogical burden is invoked both by critics and defenders of constructive approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal equality caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems in constructive texts may be worded so as to appear identical to classical theorems, yet their hypotheses or definitions have been 'tampered with' so that the apparent equality is only verbal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should beware that terms like 'continuous' may carry different technical content in a constructive setting (e.g., meaning uniform continuity), and that such verbal equality can mislead about substantive strength or applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodman–Myhill / Diaconescu theorem (choice implies LEM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom of choice (in certain forms) implies the law of excluded middle (LEM); understanding this relies on the constructive distinction between finite and 'subfinite' sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructively, a set that 'has either one or two elements (we don't know which)' cannot be called finite; finding choice functions in such contexts requires 'full' choice and can yield LEM. The proof techniques and quantifier nature are important for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive distinction: finite vs subfinite
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructive mathematics, 'finite' and 'subfinite' differ: e.g., a collection that has 'either one or two elements (we don't know which)' is not constructively finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction matters when applying choice principles; extracting elements from equivalence classes or collections with undecided cardinality requires nontrivial (and potentially nonconstructive) choice, with implications for LEM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme Value Theorem (EVT) non-constructivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical EVT (existence of a maximum of a continuous function on [0,1]) does not hold constructively in general — one cannot always constructively identify the maximizing point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples use reals a for which neither a ≥ 0 nor a ≤ 0 is known; functions like f(x)=ax have sup = max(0,a) but lack a constructively capturable maximizer. This illustrates clash between verificationist quantifier interpretations and classical existence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited Principle of Omniscience (LPO) and trichotomy
rubrics_metrics.description: LPO is a weaker nonconstructive principle than full LEM and is equivalent to trichotomy for sequences/real numbers in constructive contexts; it is a primary target of Bishop's criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LPO formulated as 'searching a sequence of integers to see whether they all vanish' connects to trichotomy (a<0 or a=0 or a>0). Failure of such principles enables construction of intuitionistic counterexamples to classical theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two conceptions of constructivism: numerical vs anti-LEM
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructivism can be understood in at least two ways: (1) numerical constructivism (seek greater numerical meaning; companion to classical math) and (2) anti-LEM constructivism (seek elimination of LEM; alternative to classical math).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction clarifies tensions in Bishop's own writings and the positions of other constructivists (Heyting, Billinge). It affects how one interprets criticisms of classical results and the permissibility of nonconstructive intermediate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-LEM vs post-LEM numerical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-LEM numerical meaning: mathematics fully constructive from base objects up; post-LEM numerical meaning: results that have undeniable numerical or computational meaning but rely on LEM at intermediate stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many important results (e.g., Archimedes' volume, Leibniz calculus, Hilbert's variational arguments, Connes' infinitesimals, Calabi–Yau metrics) are described as post-LEM — they may be nonconstructive in foundation but yield computationally meaningful conclusions. The article discusses whether such post-LEM content is acceptable or can be 'constructivized.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic modeling / Hilbertian defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert's position: one may use nonconstructive formal machinery (including LEM) to prove formally predictive/real propositions, treating formal mathematics as a route to the real via the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nonconstructive methods yield no numerically testable falsehoods, their use may be acceptable; Avigad terms this 'syntactic modeling'. Discussion includes whether classical proofs can be made constructive or whether some results resist such conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof mining / extracting numerical content
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques (e.g., proof mining) aim to extract constructive/numerical content from nonconstructive proofs using logical tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work by Avigad, Kohlenbach, Oliva is cited as showing how post-LEM arguments can sometimes yield explicit bounds/witnesses; this bears on debates about acceptability of nonconstructive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heyting's conciliatory stance on intuitionism vs classical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Heyting endorsed studying intuitionism as part of mathematics and did not treat it as an outright alternative to classical mathematics, implying constructivist goals can be complementary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This challenges a purely anti-LEM reading of intuitionism and forms part of the burden on constructivists to explain apparent endorsements of classical methods (e.g., hyperreals) by constructive-aligned figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'test-for-equality' constructions in constructive reworkings
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive reformulations (e.g., Beeson on Euclid) avoid constructions that depend on deciding equality (tests relying on LEM), requiring alternate proofs that do not use such case-splitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beeson’s reformulation of Euclid shows much can be made constructively acceptable, but raises questions about whether classical methods prior to reformulation were lacking in meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical critique of classical realism (Pourciau's 'phlogiston' metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical mathematics presumes mathematical assertions are true or false independently of our knowledge, a hidden belief that underlies acceptance of proofs by contradiction and other classical techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pourciau argues this belief creates a classical worldview that may be 'shattering' when questioned; the article uses this to frame debates about standards of meaning and civility in philosophical discourse.
